42867371.text: Background Artificial intelligence (AI) systems have demonstrated non-inferiority to radiologists for prostate cancer detection on MRI, but evidence in global diagnostic and population-based screening settings remains limited. Purpose To determine whether an AI system can achieve diagnostic performance comparable to radiology readings for detecting Gleason grade group ≥2 prostate cancer on MRI in external diagnostic and screening datasets. Materials and Methods In the SCARLET-1 retrospective validation study, prostate MRIs from adults with suspected prostate cancer (January 2012-October 2024) were used to evaluate an AI system, with external testing in diagnostic (PRIME) and organized screening settings (STHLM3-MRI and IP1-PROSTAGRAM). The primary outcome was agreement between AI assessments and standard-of-care diagnoses of Gleason grade group ≥2 cancer, with diagnostic interchangeability defined relative to the estimated agreement of an average radiologist. Secondary outcomes included area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) across datasets and subgroups. Results 22,445 examinations (21,252 male patients; median age, 66 years [IQR 60-71]) were included: 20,471 prostate MRI examinations (19,278 patients; 26 cities, 14 countries) for AI training and internal testing, and 1974 patients (20 external cities, 12 countries) for external testing. External AUCs were 0.86 (95% CI: 0.83, 0.90) in PRIME, 0.89 (95% CI: 0.86, 0.92) in STHLM3-MRI, and 0.84 (95% CI: 0.70, 0.95) in IP1-PROSTAGRAM. The primary outcome was 83.0% (395 of 476; adjusted 95% CI: 78.8%, 87.0%), 87.9% (974 of 1108; adjusted 95% CI: 85.6%, 90.3%), and 87.7% (342 of 390; adjusted 95% CI: 83.6%, 91.5%), respectively, meeting prespecified interchangeability criteria in all datasets. Subgroup performance was consistent across age, risk, cancer location and ethnicity (mean ΔAUC, 0.02), but varied substantially across 25 sites (28% with AUC<0.80; 32% with AUC ≥0.90) and by image quality (AUC, 0.78-0.88). Conclusion AI demonstrated diagnostic performance comparable to that of radiology readings across external diagnostic and screening datasets.

42874221.label: Background
42874221.text: Pediatric metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) prevalence is approximately 10%, but ultrasound fat quantification lacks validation. This study evaluated the diagnostic performance of quantitative ultrasound-derived estimated fat fraction (USFF) against magnetic resonance imaging proton density fat fraction (MRI-PDFF) in children with suspected MASLD.

42874221.label: Methods
42874221.text: This prospective single-center study enrolled 65 children aged 6-18 years with suspected MASLD. USFF, tissue attenuation imaging (TAI), tissue scatter distribution imaging (TSI), hepato-renal index (EzHRI), and shear wave elastography (SWE) were measured on a Samsung R10 Prestige platform; 3.0 T MRI-PDFF served as reference. Steatosis was graded using pediatric PDFF thresholds. Diagnostic performance was assessed by ROC analysis with DeLong comparisons and internally validated by bootstrap resampling; agreement by Bland-Altman analysis; inter-operator reproducibility assessed in a randomly selected 30-child subset.

42874221.label: Results
42874221.text: Among 65 children (48 boys; median age 11.2 years), 20 were classified as S0, 29 as S1, and 16 as S2-3. USFF AUCs were 0.941 (≥S1) and 0.960 (≥S2), higher than EzHRI and SWE, and similar to TAI (0.903, 0.957) and TSI (0.900, 0.880). USFF strongly correlated with MRI-PDFF (ρ = 0.906) but systematically underestimated PDFF (mean bias - 3.13%; non-parametric limits of agreement - 14.51% to + 4.24%). In an exploratory analysis, younger children (<12 years) showed larger bias (-4.00% vs - 1.82%, p = 0.029) with similar AUC point estimates.

42874221.label: Conclusions
42874221.text: USFF shows high diagnostic performance (AUC > 0.94) for pediatric MASLD, but its 3.13% underestimation and wide non-parametric limits of agreement warrant caution. USFF may serve as a practical tool for categorical steatosis grading in children with suspected MASLD, and the proposed thresholds require external validation before clinical use.

42888271.label: Background
42888271.text: Matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) are elevated in aortic aneurysm (AA), where older age is a risk factor. The relationship among aging, aortic MMP activity, and AA development has not been systematically evaluated. This study leveraged MMP-targeted molecular imaging to investigate how aging affects aortic MMP activity, aneurysm development, and survival.

42888271.label: Results
42888271.text: AA development and animal survival were monitored for 28 days after Angiotensin (Ang)-II infusion in 8-10-week-old (young) and > 51-week-old (old) apolipoprotein E (Apoe)-/- mice. Old animals' survival at 28 days was significantly lower than that of young Ang-II-infused Apoe-/- mice (P < 0.05). 64Cu-RYM2 PET/CT showed significantly higher aortic MMP activation before and 1 week after Ang-II infusion in old compared to young Apoe-/- mice. The 64Cu-RYM2 signal was significantly higher in animals that did not survive 28 days than in those that did (P < 0.01). MMP activity significantly increased after Ang-II infusion and correlated with aortic macrophage infiltration. The increase in MMP activity preceded aortic dissection. Finally, MMP activity was heterogeneous along the aorta of control and Ang-II-infused young and old Apoe-/- mice, and of old wild-type mice.

42888271.label: Conclusions
42888271.text: Aging is associated with increased MMP activity along the aorta and worse AA survival. MMP-targeted molecular imaging provides insights regarding aneurysm survival prospects in this exploratory cohort. Combining MMP inhibitors and tracers may help prevent and track aneurysm growth, dissection, and rupture.

42912571.text: A 3-year-old girl with high-risk neuroblastoma underwent 18 F-MFBG PET/CT for therapy response evaluation as part of a clinical trial. The scan revealed focal increased uptake in the pineal gland, which was also observed on a concurrent 68 Ga-DOTATATE PET/CT. Brain MRI showed no signs of metastasis, and importantly, follow-up 18 F-MFBG PET/CT demonstrated consistently elevated uptake in the same region without interval change. These combined findings, negative MRI, concordant physiological 68 Ga-DOTATATE uptake, and stable appearance on serial 18 F-MFBG PET/CT, support the interpretation of this pineal gland activity as a physiological normal variant rather than a pathologic lesion.

42949521.text: Purpose To develop and evaluate an interpretable CT spatial phenotype associated with extrapancreatic perineural invasion (EPNI) in resected pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma. Materials and Methods This multicenter study included training, internal testing, neoadjuvant testing, retrospective external testing, prospective external testing, and The Cancer Imaging Archive (TCIA) sets. The Preoperative Risk of Perineural High-risk Extension in Tumors (PROPHET) model and threshold were locked before testing. Performance was assessed with area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) and threshold metrics. Six radiologists compared unaided and assisted readings. A stratified Cox model related PROPHET risk to survival, adjusting for age, sex, tumor size, carbohydrate antigen 19-9, nodal category, and differentiation. Results Among 1854 patients (median age, 63 years; 1131 male), AUCs were 0.92 (95% CI: 0.86, 0.96) in prospective external testing, 0.85 (95% CI: 0.75, 0.93) in retrospective external testing, 0.90 (95% CI: 0.83, 0.95) after neoadjuvant therapy, 0.99 (95% CI: 0.98, >0.99) in internal testing, and 0.80 (95% CI: 0.68, 0.93) in TCIA. TCIA sensitivity and specificity were 24 of 30 (80%) and two of 19 (11%). Assistance increased mean sensitivity to 93% from 82% and reduced reading time to 3.02 minutes from 3.64 minutes per patient (both Holm-adjusted P < .001). Higher PROPHET risk was associated with shorter survival (adjusted hazard ratio, 1.95; 95% CI: 1.53, 2.47; nominal P < .001). Conclusion PROPHET provides a CT-visible tumor-vessel spatial phenotype associated with pathologically confirmed EPNI.

42951721.text: Adult spondylodiscitis is an infection of the intervertebral disc and adjacent vertebral bodies that may progress to paravertebral extension, epidural involvement, spinal instability, sepsis, and neurological compromise. Because clinical symptoms and laboratory markers are often nonspecific, imaging is central to diagnosis, assessment of disease extent, biopsy planning, and selective evaluation of treatment response. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) remains the first-line anatomical technique for early marrow, disc, epidural, and paraspinal disease, while computed tomography (CT) is valuable for osseous destruction, instability, and biopsy guidance. Molecular imaging complements these modalities by depicting biological activity rather than structure alone. Fluorine-18 fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography/computed tomography ([18F]FDG PET/CT) is the most established molecular technique, offering high diagnostic performance, whole-body evaluation for multifocal or metastatic infection, and support for management when MRI is contraindicated, equivocal, or difficult to interpret after surgery. Its main limitations are limited pathogen specificity, uptake in sterile inflammatory or reparative processes, heterogeneous interpretation criteria, and uncertain thresholds for treatment monitoring. Emerging approaches, including hybrid positron emission tomography/magnetic resonance imaging (PET/MRI), fibroblast activation protein inhibitor (FAPI) tracers, pathogen-targeted radiopharmaceuticals, quantitative PET biomarkers, and artificial intelligence (AI), remain investigational and require prospective validation of diagnostic and clinical utility. This review summarizes current evidence, clinical applications, limitations, and future directions for molecular imaging in spondylodiscitis.

42986771.text: The axilla is a pyramid-shaped space containing tissues of various origins including adipose, neural, vascular, cutaneous, myogenic, and lymphatic structures. Axillary masses are typically identified when patients present with palpable areas of concern or during imaging for breast cancer screening or staging. Breast imagers frequently encounter axillary masses while evaluating the axillary region at mammography and US. While reactive lymphadenopathy represents the most common cause of axillary lymph node enlargement, lymph node metastasis from breast cancer is a common cause of axillary masses requiring clinical evaluation. Recent immunization, particularly COVID-19 vaccination, is an important cause of unilateral axillary lymphadenopathy. Additional causes beyond metastatic lymphadenopathy must be considered in the differential diagnosis, including benign and malignant entities arising from accessory breast tissue, adipocytic, neurogenic, vascular, infectious, traumatic, and cutaneous origins. Understanding axillary anatomy is essential for developing a comprehensive differential diagnosis and determining appropriate management strategies. Systematic assessment of characteristic imaging and clinical findings, combined with thorough correlation with patient history and symptoms, enables accurate diagnosis. US serves as the primary imaging modality for mass assessment and biopsy guidance. Depending on the differential diagnosis, mammography, CT, and MRI provide supplementary information to better define mass origin and extent. Definitive diagnosis often requires histopathologic analysis. A systematic approach ensures accurate diagnosis and optimal management of axillary masses.

43002571.text: We present dual-tracer 18F-FDG and 18F-PSMA (prostate-specific membrane antigen) PET/CT findings in a 75-year-old man with prior scrotal extramammary Paget disease who developed diffuse bone and lymph node lesions. L1 vertebral biopsy initially favored metastatic prostatic acinar adenocarcinoma, but serum prostate-specific antigen was 0.567 ng/mL and prostate biopsies were benign. PET/CT showed intense FDG and PSMA uptake in widespread osseous and nodal lesions, whereas the prostate showed no focal FDG uptake or abnormal PSMA uptake. This discordant imaging pattern, together with clinical and pathologic correlation, supported metastatic scrotal extramammary Paget disease rather than prostate cancer.

43012971.text: Liver cirrhosis is a major risk factor for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), and accurate risk stratification of cirrhotic nodules remains a clinical challenge. During hepatocarcinogenesis, regenerative and dysplastic nodules undergo heterogeneous alterations in hepatocyte function, transporter expression, vascular architecture, and tissue composition. However, conventional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) assessment of intranodular signal heterogeneity largely relies on subjective visual interpretation and lacks standardized and reproducible quantitative biomarkers. Gadoxetic acid disodium (Gd-EOB-DTPA)-enhanced MRI provides functional information during the hepatobiliary phase by reflecting hepatocyte-specific uptake mediated by organic anion transporting polypeptides. Impaired transporter expression during malignant transformation is associated with reduced contrast uptake and may contribute to spatially heterogeneous contrast distribution. Quantitative T1 mapping enables voxel-wise measurement of absolute T1 relaxation times, thereby providing an objective and quantitative approach to tissue characterization. However, most existing studies have primarily focused on mean T1 values or global reduction rates, while intranodular spatial heterogeneity remains insufficiently explored. MRI-based heterogeneity analysis may complement conventional mean-value analysis by capturing regional variations within lesions. However, direct evidence on T1 mapping-derived heterogeneity in cirrhotic nodules remains limited, and its incremental value over mean T1 values for reflecting hepatocellular function or early malignant transformation has not been established. Quantitative heterogeneity descriptors, including standard deviation, coefficient of variation, histogram-based parameters, and texture features, can objectively characterize the magnitude and distribution of spatial T1 variation and provide a quantitative framework for assessing intralesional heterogeneity. This review summarizes the biological rationale, technical principles, and emerging evidence regarding Gd-EOB-DTPA-enhanced T1 mapping for the assessment of intranodular heterogeneity. It further discusses its potential role in malignant transformation risk stratification of cirrhotic nodules, current limitations, and future directions for clinical translation.

43084071.label: Objective
43084071.text: To evaluate the incremental value of computed tomography (CT)-derived body composition indices for preoperative prediction of lymphovascular invasion (LVI) in clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC).

43084071.label: Methods
43084071.text: This single-center retrospective study included 315 patients with pathologically confirmed ccRCC who underwent preoperative multiphasic CT between May 2020 and December 2024. Patients were randomly divided (7:3) into training (n = 223; 81 LVI-positive) and internal validation (n = 92; 28 LVI-positive) cohorts. Postoperative histopathology served as the reference standard for LVI. Clinical characteristics, conventional CT features, and body composition indices were collected. Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression and multivariable logistic regression were used for predictor selection and model construction. Model performance was assessed using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves, calibration curves, and decision curve analysis (DCA).

43084071.label: Results
43084071.text: The clinicoradiological model included body mass index (BMI; odds ratio [OR], 0.758; p < 0.001), neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR; OR, 1.765; p = 0.010), and size (OR, 1.629; p < 0.001). The body composition model included skeletal muscle index (SMI; OR, 0.951; p = 0.005) and total adipose tissue index (TATI; OR, 0.977; p < 0.001); the combined model included all five predictors. In the training cohort, areas under the ROC curve (AUCs) were 0.852, 0.730, and 0.851 for the clinicoradiological, body composition, and combined models, respectively. The combined model did not significantly outperform the clinicoradiological model (p = 0.917). In the internal validation cohort, the clinicoradiological and combined models had AUCs of 0.778 and 0.774, respectively (p = 0.609). In both cohorts, confidence intervals for Brier score differences included zero, indicating no apparent improvement in calibration with the addition of body composition indices. DCA showed no consistent advantage in net benefit.

43084071.label: Conclusion
43084071.text: Although SMI and TATI are associated with LVI in the standalone body composition model, they provide no clear incremental predictive value beyond the clinicoradiological model. Findings from this cohort support prioritizing multicenter external validation and clinical impact assessment of the more parsimonious clinicoradiological model.

43086471.label: Background
43086471.text: Accurately identifying patients with locally advanced pancreatic cancer (LAPC) who are unlikely to respond to neoadjuvant FOLFIRINOX therapy remains a critical unmet need. Conventional anatomic imaging often fails to capture early changes in tumor biology. In contrast, dual-time-point ¹⁸F-FDG PET/CT provides a functional assessment of tumor glycolytic dynamics through the retention index (RI). However, the utility of pretreatment RI for predicting treatment response and overall survival (OS) in LAPC has not been systematically evaluated. This study aimed to assess the predictive value of baseline RI derived from dual-time-point ¹⁸F-FDG PET/CT in LAPC patients receiving neoadjuvant therapy.

43086471.label: Results
43086471.text: This retrospective analysis included 42 LAPC patients who underwent pretreatment dual-time-point ¹⁸F-FDG PET/CT followed by neoadjuvant FOLFIRINOX. The RI was significantly higher in patients who experienced clinical progression (n = 24, 57.1%) compared to non-progressors (median: 57.28% vs. 0.57%; P < 0.0001). Among the 37 patients with complete survival follow-up, time-dependent ROC analysis identified an optimal RI cutoff of 23.5% for predicting 2-year mortality. Patients with a high RI (≥ 23.5%) had a significantly shorter median OS (21.5 months vs. not reached; log-rank P = 0.00059). In a multivariable Cox regression model adjusting for CA19-9, histologic grade, tumor location, treatment duration, and SUV parameters, a low RI (< 23.5%) remained independently associated with a reduced risk of death (HR = 0.036; 95% CI: 0.002-0.83; P = 0.038).

43086471.label: Conclusions
43086471.text: Pretreatment RI derived from dual-time-point ¹⁸F-FDG PET/CT is a robust and independent predictor of both treatment resistance and overall survival in LAPC patients undergoing neoadjuvant FOLFIRINOX therapy. Its strong discriminatory performance supports its potential for early risk stratification and personalized treatment selection. Prospective validation in larger cohorts is warranted.
